quests.hint: A failing company sells off all its equipment, inventory, and property to pay back what it owes before closing for good.
quests.explanation: -ATE turns the noun LIQUID into the verb LIQUIDATE, to convert assets into cash, often to settle debts.
quests.instruction: Which suffix turns this noun into a verb?

quests.hint: An investor spreads money across stocks, bonds, real estate, and gold instead of putting everything into one company.
quests.explanation: DIVERSIFICATION combines DI- (a form of DIS-, 'apart') with VERSE ('turn') and -IFICATION (a form of -IFY plus -ATION), spreading investments across different, varied options to reduce risk.
quests.meaningBreakdown: DI (prefix, 'apart') + VERSE (root, 'turn') + IFICATION (suffix, forms a noun of process)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: The final legal step where a bankrupt store's remaining assets are officially converted to cash and distributed to creditors.
quests.explanation: -ATION forms LIQUIDATION from LIQUID, the process of converting assets into cash. -MENT wouldn't fit — 'liquidment' isn't standard English, since LIQUID specifically takes -ATION here through the verb LIQUIDATE.
quests.meaningBreakdown: LIQUID (root) + ATION (suffix, forms a noun of process)
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A scientist insists that any claim in her report must be backed by numbers that can actually be measured and counted.
quests.explanation: -IFY (to make) plus -ABLE (capable of being) combine with QUANTITY to form QUANTIFIABLE, capable of being expressed or measured as a specific amount.
quests.instruction: Which suffix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: A teacher wants to see students improve their reading speed by a clear number of words per minute this semester, not just 'try harder.'
quests.explanation: MEASURABLE is MEASURE + -ABLE, capable of being measured in specific, concrete terms.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A government office whose entire job is writing and enforcing the rules that food and drug companies must follow.
quests.explanation: -ORY, a suffix related to -ARY, forms REGULATORY from REGULATE, relating to the making or enforcing of rules. -ARY wouldn't fit here — English settled on REGULATORY, not 'regulatary,' for this particular word.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A speech therapist works with a child to help him pronounce his 'r' and 's' sounds more clearly.
quests.explanation: -TION turns the verb ARTICULATE into the noun ARTICULATION, the act of pronouncing words clearly, or expressing an idea precisely.
quests.instruction: Which suffix turns this verb into a noun?

quests.hint: A report that covers every single angle of the problem, from history to causes to possible solutions, leaving nothing out.
quests.explanation: COMPREHENSIVE comes from COMPREHEND, with a spelling shift, plus -IVE, covering everything relevant, complete and thorough.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A magician's trick so impossible-looking that the audience gasps, unable to believe their own eyes.
quests.explanation: IN- ('not') + CREDIBLE ('believable') = INCREDIBLE, so extraordinary it's hard to believe. UN- wouldn't fit here — 'uncredible' isn't standard English, since CREDIBLE specifically takes IN-.
quests.instruction: Which prefix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A government removes strict rules on an industry, letting companies operate with much more freedom than before.
quests.explanation: DE- ('remove') + REGULATE = DEREGULATE, to remove rules or restrictions that previously controlled an industry.
quests.instruction: Which prefix fits the meaning below?

quests.hint: After a disputed election, international observers debate whether the new government was actually chosen fairly and lawfully.
quests.explanation: LEGITIMACY is LEGITIMATE + -CY, the quality of being lawful, genuine, or properly authorized.
quests.meaningBreakdown: LEGITIMA (root) + CY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A contract clause so vaguely written that a judge rules it cannot actually be legally required of either party.
quests.explanation: -ABLE forms ENFORCEABLE from ENFORCE, capable of being legally required or carried out. Its negative, UNENFORCEABLE, is exactly what this contract clause turned out to be.
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A lawyer objects when the opposing side brings up a witness's unrelated parking tickets during a murder trial.
quests.explanation: IRRELEVANCE combines IR- ('not') with RELEVANT and -CE (a form of -ANCE), the state of having no bearing on the matter at hand. This reviews IR- from IRRELEVANT, now extended one step further into its noun form.
quests.meaningBreakdown: IR (prefix, 'not') + RELEVAN (root) + CE (suffix, forms an abstract noun)
quests.instruction: Which suffix completes this word's noun form?

quests.hint: Once the two storms merged over the ocean, meteorologists knew landfall was simply a matter of when, not if.
quests.explanation: INEVITABILITY is INEVITABLE + -ITY, the quality of being certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
quests.meaningBreakdown: INEVITABIL (root) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A city plans decades ahead, balancing economic growth with protecting its forests and water supply for future generations.
quests.explanation: -ITY forms SUSTAINABILITY from SUSTAINABLE, itself SUSTAIN + -ABLE, the overall quality or practice of meeting today's needs without harming the future. This closes Phase 8: sophisticated, real-world vocabulary built from the exact same small set of pieces used since Level 1.
quests.meaningBreakdown: SUSTAINABLE (root, itself sustain + able) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: Which suffix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A years-long conflict between two nations that no diplomat, treaty, or mediator has ever been able to resolve.
quests.explanation: IN- ('not') + TRACT ('pull, manage') + -ABLE = INTRACTABLE, so difficult to handle that it resists every effort. You met TRACT back in Phase 7 (DISTRACT, SUBTRACT, EXTRACT) — here it's paired with a prefix and suffix you also already know, on a word you've likely never seen before.
quests.instruction: Mastery: use IN- ('not'), TRACT ('pull/manage'), and -ABLE to infer this word's meaning.

quests.hint: A medical test that comes back with mixed signals, leaving doctors unable to confirm or rule out the diagnosis either way.
quests.explanation: INCONCLUSIVE layers IN- ('not') onto CONCLUSIVE, itself CON- ('completely') + CLUDE ('shut,' spelled CLUS- here) + -IVE, meaning not leading to a definite conclusion. Three word-building pieces from three different phases of this course, all stacked on one word.
quests.meaningBreakdown: IN (prefix, 'not') + CON (prefix, 'completely') + CLUS (root, 'shut') + IVE (suffix, 'having the nature of')
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A financial advisor who reviews every possible risk from every angle before recommending even a small investment.
quests.explanation: CIRCUM- ('around') + SPECT ('look') = CIRCUMSPECT, looking around carefully before acting — cautious and thorough. You've never seen CIRCUM- before, but you already know PERI- means 'around' from PERISCOPE — a reminder that more than one prefix can express a similar idea.
quests.instruction: Mastery: can you infer this new prefix's meaning from context, the way you inferred RETRO- earlier?

quests.hint: A salesperson who calls back every single week for three months, refusing to give up on landing the client.
quests.explanation: -ENT turns the verb PERSIST into the adjective PERSISTENT, continuing firmly despite difficulty or opposition.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: The quality that let an inventor fail two thousand times before finally getting the light bulb to work.
quests.explanation: PERSISTENCE is PERSISTENT + -CE, the quality of continuing firmly despite obstacles — closing a two-step family built entirely from suffixes you've used dozens of times.
quests.meaningBreakdown: PERSISTEN (root) + CE (suffix, forms an abstract noun)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A referee who calls a foul on one team for a play but lets the exact same play go unpunished for the other team minutes later.
quests.explanation: IN- ('not') + CONSISTENT ('the same throughout') = INCONSISTENT, not applying the same standard evenly. This closes out the PERSIST/CONSIST/INSIST/RESIST family — related roots, all built the same way, each branching into its own set of words.
quests.meaningBreakdown: IN (prefix, 'not') + CONSISTENT (root, itself con + sist + ent)
quests.instruction: Which prefix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A contract that spells out every single term in exact detail, leaving no room for assumption or guesswork.
quests.explanation: EX- ('out') + PLIC ('fold') = EXPLICIT, literally 'folded out' — stated clearly and directly. IM- would instead give IMPLICIT, 'folded in' — implied rather than directly stated, the opposite approach to communication.
quests.instruction: Mastery: EX- means 'out,' IM- means 'in.' Which fits a contract that states everything directly?

quests.hint: A dress code that never actually says 'no shorts' out loud, but everyone at the office just understands not to wear them.
quests.explanation: IMPLICIT is IM- ('in') + PLIC ('fold'), literally 'folded in' — understood without being directly stated.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: A locksmith cuts a second copy of a house key so both roommates can come and go independently.
quests.explanation: DU- ('two') + PLIC ('fold') + -ATE = DUPLICATE, literally 'folded twice' — an exact copy. This connects the PLIC family to the number prefixes from Phase 5: MONO-, BI-, TRI-, and now DU-, all describing quantity.
quests.meaningBreakdown: DU (prefix, 'two') + PLIC (root, 'fold') + ATE (suffix, forms a verb/adjective)
quests.instruction: Which prefix correctly completes this word?

quests.hint: A judge rules that a contract signed under threat doesn't legally count and throws the whole agreement out.
quests.explanation: IN- ('not') + VALID ('legally sound') + -ATE = INVALIDATE, to make something not valid or legally void. This is the reverse direction of transformation you've practiced all course: instead of building up from a verb to a noun, here a negated adjective becomes a brand-new verb.
quests.instruction: Which suffix turns this negated adjective into a verb?

quests.hint: A parking garage stamps your ticket to confirm you actually attended the conference, so you get the discounted rate.
quests.explanation: VALIDATION is VALID + -ATE + -ION, the act of confirming something is genuine, correct, or officially acceptable.
quests.meaningBreakdown: VALID (root) + ATION (suffix, adjective → noun of process)
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Someone forms a negative opinion about a stranger based only on their appearance, before ever speaking a single word to them.
quests.explanation: PRE- ('before') + JUDIC ('judge') = PREJUDICE, literally to judge before knowing the facts. After nearly two hundred levels, this might be the most important reminder of all: understanding how a word is built doesn't just help you pass a quiz — it helps you think more carefully about the words people use every day, including the ones that shape how we treat each other.
quests.instruction: Mastery: which prefix means 'before,' completing a word that means 'to judge in advance'?

quests.hint: A homeowner freshens up the faded walls of a room for the second time in ten years, choosing a bolder color this time.
quests.explanation: RE- + PAINT = REPAINT, the same RE- ('again') met all the way back in Level 1's REDO. Two hundred levels later, the smallest, simplest piece of this whole course is still doing exactly the same job.
quests.instruction: Final level: the very first prefix you ever learned. Which one means 'again'?

quests.hint: A scientist's theory holds up against every single experiment designed to prove it wrong, again and again, for decades.
quests.explanation: IR- ('not,' shifting before R) + REFUTE ('prove wrong') + -ABLE = IRREFUTABLE, impossible to disprove. IR- from the IN- family, a root you can reason through using inference skills, and -ABLE, one of the very first suffixes this course ever taught, back in Level 9. Every phase of this course, working together on one word.
quests.meaningBreakdown: IR (prefix, 'not') + REFUTE (root, 'prove wrong') + ABLE (suffix, 'capable of being')
quests.instruction: Final mastery check: which suffix completes this word?

quests.hint: Someone picks up a genuinely unfamiliar word next month, pauses, and realizes they can work out what it means — all on their own, without a dictionary.
quests.explanation: ACHIEVABLE is ACHIEVE + -ABLE, capable of being accomplished. That feeling — recognizing a prefix, spotting a familiar root, noticing a suffix, and piecing together a meaning independently — was always the real goal of this course, and after two hundred levels, it's now a genuinely achievable, ordinary part of how you read.
quests.instruction: One final suffix, to close the course: which one completes this word?
